run in the sense of operate or manage the system
entries.resolution: English kept: Run is EPANET's own command word, it is one word for a narrow toolbar button, and its tip names the act. Routed to a new glossary.json concept "run (a simulation)", wired to lpn, whose avoid array leads with the run-of-pipe trap and which states the two requirements the strings impose: the button must be an imperative verb, and the noun used in lpn_time_run_note, lpn_time_run_tip and lpn_time_duration must be the same word the button carries.

entries.complaint: medium, second finding on the same string: "work out" is this suite's house verb for compute, and it appears in four clock strings (lpn_time_run_tip, lpn_time_run_note, lpn_time_running, lpn_time_no_engine). Word by word it is opaque -- a phrasal verb whose parts mean neither computing nor solving -- and its everyday senses (take physical exercise; turn out well; settle a disagreement) are all more frequent than the arithmetic one. Four strings translated by one agent on four different guesses is four different verbs for one act.
readings: compute or solve the network (intended)
take exercise
turn out well in the end
negotiate or settle something
figure out by guessing
entries.resolution: English kept -- "work out" is the Simple English choice over "calculate"/"solve" and is used consistently across the clock strings. Routed to a new glossary.json concept "work out (compute)", wired to lpn, which names the three wrong senses, says one rendering must serve all four strings, and tells the agent to use the ordinary verb for calculating rather than copying the two-word English shape.

entries.complaint: medium: the tip teaches a number format by example -- "17.5 or 72.5" -- and every example uses the English decimal point. The field itself accepts a comma decimal for typed input (js/lpn-patterns.js takes <digits>,<digits>; Task 444 added it precisely because parseFloat silently truncated 2,5 to 2 in the field that sizes the whole run). So a reader in a comma locale is shown a format they do not write, in a field that would have accepted the one they do. Nothing in the English marks the digits as localisable, and an agent translating conservatively will copy them.
readings: decimal hours written with the local separator, whatever it is (intended, and what the parser accepts)
the dot is required, so a comma will be refused
17.5 as seventeen and a half hours vs. 17.5 as a clock time near half past five
entries.resolution: English kept -- it is Tom's own 2026-08-19 wording (Task 449) and it does the hard part well, pairing 17.5 with 17:30 so the two notations explain each other. The unmarked-digits problem is routed to a new glossary.json concept "decimal separator", wired to lpn, which tells agents to write their own locale's separator in an EXAMPLE (the precedent Tom set for lpn_labels_col_decimals_example, "0,000" where needed), and equally that the COLON in 17:30 is not a separator and never changes, and that a thousands separator must never be added because the parser refuses it.

entries.complaint: medium: "Color links by" is a sentence that stops at a preposition and is completed by the value of the select beside it. English tolerates that; word order, case government and RTL do not, and the translator sees only the fragment. It compounds with "Color" being verb or noun with no marker: "Color links" can be read as "the colors of links". Renamed from "Color pipes by" this session, which widens the object correctly (links are pipes, pumps and valves) but does not touch the fragment problem.
readings: choose the property by which links are colored (intended, imperative plus trailing select)
"Color links" as a noun phrase -- the colors belonging to links -- ordered by something
color the links according to something not yet named
entries.resolution: English kept. The pair lpn_color_node_field / lpn_color_link_field must stay parallel, the trailing-preposition-plus-select shape is used throughout this panel and is why the select reads as its completion on screen, and no English reader stumbles. The translator-facing half is real but belongs in the synonym channel, which is OFF-LIMITS to AI, so the diff is recorded here unwritten for Tom to approve or drop: $ec_lang_syn['lpn_color_link_field']='Color links by, Color the links according to, Show link values as colors of, Link color shows, Use this value for link color | avoid: the noun reading "the colors of links"; a rendering that cannot be completed by the value of the dropdown that follows it'. The same diff would apply to lpn_color_node_field.

entries.complaint: medium: one of the four section names in the Settings box, and the only abstract Latinate noun among them -- its siblings are "Map and page", "New elements" and "Calculation". It names no object, so it does not separate itself from "Map and page", which is also visual; a user hunting for the label and color controls has two plausible doors. It is also the kind of word that invites a phonetic loan rather than a translation in several of the low-resource languages.
readings: labels and colors -- how values are shown on the drawing (intended)
anything to do with how the page looks, which is also "Map and page"
a chart or graph feature
a 3D or animated view
entries.resolution: English kept, and NOT routed. The four section names are Tom's own groupings, given 2026-08-18 while using the box, and naming is his call; the section's two subsections are already "Node symbology" and "Link symbology", which is the standard word in QGIS, ArcGIS and Bentley and anchors the concept on screen one line below the heading. Recorded rather than resolved silently: if Tom wants a plainer word, "Symbology" is the trade term and "Labels and colors" is the Simple English one.

entries.complaint: low: "Link line thickness (pixels)" is a three-noun pile, and "link line" is not a compound English uses -- the reader has to decide whether the line belongs to the link or links something. Renamed from "Pipe line thickness" this session, which fixed the wrong-object problem (links include pumps and valves) but kept the pile.
readings: how thick the line drawn for each link is (intended)
the thickness of a line that links things
the width of a link, as a hydraulic property
entries.resolution: English kept. It sits between "Text size (pixels)" and "Symbol opacity (0 to 1)" in one column of map-appearance numbers, its unit is stated, and the neighbouring rows establish that every row is a drawing property. The hydraulic reading is unavailable because a pipe diameter is nowhere near this box and is never in pixels.

entries.complaint: low: "Data classification method" is three abstract nouns, and "classification" plus "method" is exactly the shape that gets calqued into an unreadable phrase in the low-resource languages.
readings: the rule used to cut the values into colored classes (intended)
a method of classifying the data set as a whole, e.g. by type
a security or confidentiality classification
entries.resolution: English kept, deliberately and on the record: it is this session's considered rename away from our own coinage "Range allocation" to the term the reference tools publish (ArcGIS Pro's help page is titled "Data classification methods"; QGIS calls the act "Classify"), and Tom, 2026-08-19: "Don't drop the 'method'. That's the point of this control." The security sense is out of reach beside a list of quantile / natural breaks / equal interval. The glossary already carries "equal intervals / equal counts" wired to lpn for the values inside the select.

entries.complaint: low, second finding: this note and lpn_settings_color_breaks_note say the same thing in two different sets of words ("Left alone, these limits follow the values now on the map ..." vs "Leave these blank and the colors are spread across the values now on the map ..."), one in the Visibility panel and one in the Settings box. Two English sentences for one fact are two chances to drift, and 26 languages must now keep both in step with each other.
readings: two notes describing one behaviour, deliberately worded for two places
two different behaviours, since the words differ
entries.resolution: Left alone in this pass, and recorded rather than fixed: merging them is a key-consolidation decision (which key survives, which panel borrows it), and CLAUDE.md puts consolidation in one full-suite English-only pass, never inside a sprint gate. Flagged here so the next consolidation pass finds it with the pair already named.

entries.complaint: medium: written after the pass above, so it gets the same question here. 'Net3-World' is the FILE's name and would have read as a proper noun a translator must not touch; 'World' also invites 'worldwide' or 'the whole world' rather than 'on real ground'.
readings: EPANET's Net3 with lon/lat coordinates
a worldwide network
a variant model named World
entries.resolution: Titled 'EPANET Net3, lat/lon'. 'lat/lon' is Tom's own term (Task 145) and already appears translated in the four New project rows, so this reuses a settled word instead of introducing 'World'. 'EPANET Net3' is an identity string and stays.

entries.complaint: medium: the first draft said the network 'sits on real ground', which reads as soil or terrain -- a hydraulic page is exactly where a reader might take 'ground' as ground elevation, which this sentence is not about.
readings: placed at real-world coordinates
resting on the ground surface
drawn at ground elevation
entries.resolution: 'placed in a real location' instead of 'on real ground'. 'street map' matches the word the four New project rows already use for the basemap.

entries.complaint: high: written after the pass above, so it gets the same question here. 'No time period' can be read as 'the period is unknown', 'the period is over', or 'this tool cannot do periods' -- and a reader who takes the third stops looking for the setting. A first draft also said 'no time model', which is jargon.
readings: the project's total run time is zero, so there is one moment
the period has elapsed
this calculator does not do time
entries.resolution: States the consequence and the cure in the same sentence: one moment to show, and Total run time in Settings is where to change it. 'Total run time' is quoted from lpn_time_duration, so the sentence names a control the reader can actually find; if that label is retranslated, this string must follow it.

entries.complaint: Reported independently by es, fr, it, ro and hr: the title is a proper noun plus the project-mode name, so in a language that keeps 'lat/lon' literal there is nothing left to translate and the identical-to-english gate fires on a correct value.
readings: correctly identical, and the exempt list is what is missing
a translation defect needing a different rendering
entries.resolution: Not an English defect -- a TOOLING defect, and an expensive one. Three agents distorted a correct title to get past the gate (hr invented a phrase inconsistent with its own other mode-name strings, bg swapped the comma for an em dash, de renamed a correct 'XY' to 'XY-Ebene'). All three reverted; lpn_ex_net3_world_title and lpn_xymap added to translation_exempt_keys.json. A gate that forces a wrong translation is worse than no gate.

entries.complaint: Reported by tr and sw: 'Drop' is a deliberately narrow column heading, and neither language has a short word that is unmistakably 'leave this label off the map' rather than 'a fall in head or elevation' -- the hydraulic sense being live on this very page.
readings: a word for omit/skip
a word cognate with a hydraulic drop
entries.resolution: The English is right and the glossary trap term already warns about exactly this; every language that reported it chose the omit sense correctly. Recorded because two independent reports on one heading is the threshold at which a third would make it an English problem. Turkish notes its rendering is longer than the English and wants a native check for column fit.

entries.complaint: 'Pretty (rounded)' names a GIS class-break algorithm, but 'Pretty' alone gives no hint the subject is rounding rather than appearance, so a translator has to already know the convention.
readings: tidy/rounded numbers
attractive
entries.resolution: Referred to Tom, and it is a naming call, which CLAUDE.md reserves for him. 'Pretty' is QGIS's own word for the class-break method that rounds limits to tidy numbers. Keeping it costs a guess in every language that does not know that tool; changing it costs recognisability for everyone who does. Nothing shipped wrong -- the '(rounded)' parenthetical carries the meaning, which is why 25 languages rendered it correctly. One line from Tom closes it.

entries.complaint: In Hindi the glossary's instruction -- tie the Run button to the same root as 'Total run time' -- produces the exact word the shipped Play button already uses, so Run and Play would carry one label.
readings: a distinct verb for Run (compute/work out)
the glossary's root, colliding with Play
entries.resolution: The agent chose correctly and several other languages hit the same fork independently (ar, ur, fa, he all separated Run from Play). The glossary's 'run (a simulation)' entry should say that Run must not collide with Play in the target language, and that separating them wins where it would. Worth adding before the next sprint.

entries.complaint: The section heading has no stated scope, so it is unclear whether it means visualizing generally -- overlapping the View menu -- or specifically the colour-and-label controls it contains.
readings: the colour and label styling controls
a general 'ways of viewing the map' heading
entries.resolution: Tom ruled on this word 2026-08-19, keeping Visualization over Symbology: 'visualization is more specific to this application, where we are trying to quickly visualize the performance of a large system instead of poring through reams of numbers.' The scope ambiguity is real but the alternative is jargon; the section's own contents resolve it on screen.

entries.complaint: Second report on this heading, after ps: 'Visualization' has no settled Burmese equivalent the way the neighbouring section names do, so the agent coined a compound rather than translating an established term.
readings: a coined compound meaning visual display
a transliterated loanword
entries.resolution: Same ruling as the ps report. Tom chose Visualization over Symbology 2026-08-19 precisely because it is specific to what this page is for -- seeing a large system's performance at a glance instead of reading numbers -- and Symbology is the more jargonistic word, not the less. A coined compound in a low-resource language is the expected and correct outcome for a concept with no local term; the register rule says describe the thing plainly, which is what happened.
